classification.difficultyReason: Parts a, b and d are routine bias and sample-size explanations. Part c needs recognising survivorship bias in a new context, which sets the hardest demand. The context is less obscure than the aircraft case.

content.prompt: Explain why the following sampling methods may result in an unrepresentative sample:

children.label: a
children.prompt: A radio station asks listeners to phone in to say whether they support a new stadium.

answer.short: Volunteer bias: only listeners who choose to phone in are counted, and they may feel more strongly than those who don't.
answer.worked: Volunteer bias: the method relies on listeners choosing to phone in. Listeners with strong views are more likely to respond, so their opinions may differ from those of the listeners who do not call.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Finding out how Australians spend their weekends by interviewing people at a golf course on a Saturday morning.

answer.short: Selection bias: people at a golf course on Saturday are spending the weekend playing golf, so golf is likely to be overestimated.
answer.worked: Selection bias: people at a golf course on a Saturday morning are already spending their weekend playing golf. They do not represent Australians generally, so the sample is likely to overestimate how many spend weekends playing golf.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Judging how well new cafés in Melbourne do by interviewing the owners of cafés that have been open for 10 years or more.

answer.short: Survivorship bias: cafés that closed are ignored, so their success is likely to be overestimated.
answer.worked: Survivorship bias: cafés that have been open for 10 years or more are the successful cases. New cafés that failed and closed are ignored, so the sample is likely to overestimate how well new cafés do.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Asking 3 randomly chosen students which lunch item the school canteen should sell more of.

answer.short: Small sample size: 3 students may miss the variety of preferences and results may vary greatly by chance. Size alone does not make the method biased.
answer.worked: Small sample size: only 3 students are asked, so the sample may miss the variety of preferences in the school and the results may vary greatly by chance. The students are randomly chosen, so the method itself is not biased; the sample is simply too small.
